name: Tsotso
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Dalgish, Gerard M. 1976, The morphophonemics of the OluTsootso dialect of (Olu)Luyia, PhD diss. (261 pp., ProQuest) — not openly accessible

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerry [Gerard M.]. 1975. Nasal interactions and Bantu vowel-initial roots: the morphological or phonological solution? Proceedings of the Sixth Conference on African Linguistics, OSU Working Papers in Linguistics 20: 68-74.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Silent on stress; 'final accented a' (p. 72) refers to the tonal accent of imperatives, not word stress. Data from 10 months with Orren Tsuma, OluTsootso speaker; Guthrie E.32b.

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerry [Gerard M.]. 1974. Arguments for a unified treatment of y-initial and vowel-initial roots in Olutsootso. Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 4(2): 76-90.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login: WID Offsite Storage P1.S785 (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Nothing about word stress. Only prominence remarks are notational footnotes: fn. 3 'The capitalized segments indicate that raised tone and accent are on that syllable' (p. 89) and fn. 10 'The capitalized and underlined vowels in these paradigms indicate that high tone and accent fall on these vowels, and that all preceding tones must be low' (p. 90) — tonal (H-tone/accent) notation for imperative paradigms, no stress rule.
Phonology section is Luwanga-based; nothing on tone or stress; lists Tsotso only as one of the Luhya-proper dialects.

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143.
sources.note: Tsootso only in fn. 11: 'See Dalgish (1986) for discussion of related phenomena in Tsootso' (vowel shortening). No stress statement; survey of Luyia verbal tone melodies (Bukusu, Idakho, Khayo, Marachi, Nyala-West, Tiriki, Tura, Wanga etc.).

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2013. Verb tone in Bantu languages: micro-typological patterns and research methods. Africana Linguistica 19: 137-234.
sources.note: Tsotso appears only in list (50) 'Tsotso (Dalgish 1974: 85-88)' among languages where Imperative/Subjunctive + OM is a tonally distinct construction, and in the references (Dalgish 1974). No stress statement.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2009. Khayo verbal tonology. Africana Linguistica 15: 77-129.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey); publisher (doi, likely paywalled))
sources.note: Khayo, not Tsotso. Single Tsotso mention: 'Some other Luyia dialects, including Marachi and Tsotso, and a number of other Bantu languages have the final vowel -a in this context (Marlo 2008b, Meeussen 1967, Polak 1986)' (Imperative + OP). No stress statement for any variety; 'penultimate' only as tone-docking site.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2008. Tura verbal tonology. Studies in African Linguistics 37(2): 153-243.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Tura (different Luyia variety); no mention of Tsotso at all; not used.

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerard M. 1986. /-a-/ reduction phenomena in Luyia. Studies in African Linguistics 17(2): 155-176.
sources.note: Silent on stress and tone; discusses OluTsootso vowel length (compensatory lengthening, pre-nasal-cluster lengthening) and segmental morphophonemics of the distant-past /-a-/ only.

sources.citation: PHOIBLE 2.0, language page tsot1241 (inventory 'Lutsootso (GM 1441)', 31 segments) and Glottolog 5.3 languoid tsot1241 / reference pages
sources.note: No suprasegmental information; PHOIBLE inventory sourced from Dalgish 1976. Glottolog descriptive refs for Tsotso: Dalgish 1974, 1975, 1976 (+ Kanyoro 1983 as MED).

sources.citation: Amweye, Makomereh-Kalerwa. 2009. Language and gender: a study on how Tsotso expresses gender. MA thesis, University of Nairobi.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Only other Tsotso-specific thesis located; a Kenyan MA typically opens with a language-background chapter that may repeat a stress/tone remark, but the topic is sociolinguistic so the chance is low.

sources.citation: Kanyoro, Rachel Msimbi Angogo. 1983. Unity in diversity: a linguistic survey of the Abaluyia of western Kenya. Wien: Afro-Pub (Beiträge zur Afrikanistik), 322 pp. [publication of her 1980 University of Texas at Austin PhD dissertation]
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Comparative/dialect survey covering all Luyia varieties including Tsotso (Glottolog MED, 7 pp. on Tsotso); a comparative phonology overview may contain a general statement on Luyia tone vs. stress applicable to Tsotso.

sources.citation: Dalgish, Gerard Matthew. 1976. The morphophonemics of the OluTsootso dialect of (Olu)Luyia: issues and implications. PhD dissertation, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, vi+255 pp.

sources.access_detail: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: The only full phonology of Tsotso (Glottolog hhtype phonology; source of PHOIBLE's Lutsootso inventory); if any statement on stress/accent vs. tone exists for Tsotso it is here, presumably in the introductory chapter on the sound system and in the treatment of vowel length and tone.

sources.citation: Sample, Ward Arthur. 1976. The application of rules in the phonology of Olukisa. PhD dissertation, Indiana University, ix+263 pp.

sources.note: Phonology of Kisa, Tsotso's closest sister in Glottolog (Kisa-Marama-Tsotso); would supply the nearest-relative statement on stress/tone if Tsotso itself stays unreachable (identity caveat: Kisa lks, not Tsotso).
